title: 24th Sitting of third session of 2025
summary: The 24th sitting of the third session of 2025 opened on 25 November 2025, presided over by the Speaker. Most of this part is the debate on the Budget Review Committee's report on the 2026 state budget: government-aligned members defended it as a plan to repay debt and fund island projects, while MDP members said it lacks a clear plan, detail on projects and enough development spending. After a break (10:28 to 11:02) the Speaker closed the budget debate, since the remaining speakers were in committee, and the House began debating the whole-House committee's report on a constitutional amendment bill that would abolish atoll councils. No vote was taken in this part; the present-members count in the text is garbled so it is left blank. Five members spoke in the closing stretch of the debate on the whole-House committee report on the government's Constitution amendment bill, which would abolish the atoll councils. Speakers argued over democracy, decentralisation and what happens to atoll council staff, and the chair then closed the debate. After a recess (11:40 to 13:33) the House passed the 2026 state budget, about MVR 64.2 billion, by 74 votes to 12, and then passed the Constitution amendment bill by 75 votes to 12. The next sitting was set for 9:00 on Wednesday 26 November 2025.

speakers.name: Hussain Shareef
positions: Said earlier governments' borrowing is why so much of the budget goes to debt, and argued Malé residents most need housing.
On the constitutional bill, said abolishing atoll councils removes no service from citizens and that empowered island councils can act directly.
Rejected the 'rubber stamp' description of PNC members, saying they vote on national interest.

speakers.name: Ibrahim Falah
positions: Defended the budget, saying revenue is projected near MVR 40 billion and about two thirds of spending is recurrent.
Pointed to debts and unpaid bills left by the previous MDP government and said future debt-repayment needs are smaller.
On the constitutional bill, said the committee debated it at length and the opposition's requested amendment on recall votes was already put to a vote.

speakers.name: Dr. Ahmed Shamheed
positions: Said the 2026 budget shows no clear direction or development plan, and that rising debt and recurrent spending crowd out projects.
Argued bond and debt repayments and large announced projects are not matched by the budget's spending detail.
Said health-sector staff such as those at IGMH have had pay reduced.

speakers.name: Mohamed Shamin Habeeb
positions: Supported the budget and listed works under way or planned in his constituency, such as a police station, youth centre, council office and harbour.
Said he expects the projects to be completed within President Muizzu's term.

speakers.name: Ameen Faisal
positions: Raised concern that the budget gives no project-level detail for his constituency, citing Auditor General and Maldives Monetary Authority advice.
Said islands in his constituency still lack basic services such as water and sewerage and argued budget shares should be more equal.

speakers.name: Ahmed Riyaz
positions: Called it a hopeful budget for Kolhumadulu atoll, citing hospitals, police stations, youth centres, roads and resort development.
Said fixed figures per project in the budget are not needed and praised the government's progress.

speakers.name: Mohamed Ibrahim
positions: Said the budget shows few ways to raise revenue, salaries remain low and government workers' protests have had no answer.
Said overseas Aasandha spending is still high and the government has many posts but low productivity.
Argued foreign relations have weakened and government events are loud but not efficient.

speakers.name: Hussain Hameed
positions: Said the budget works toward self-reliance and defended building airports on smaller islands.
Urged more revenue sources than tourism, citing the China trade agreement, and said Aasandha waste should be cut.
Said pensions should not go to people who already draw state salaries.

speakers.name: Ashraf Rasheed
positions: Called the budget hopeful, saying it targets housing, education and health problems raised across the country.
Said this government does not use supplementary budgets, which he said the previous government did.
Cited work starting on long-neglected islands in his constituency such as Rathafandhoo.

speakers.name: Ahmed Naseer
positions: Said the budget meets its fiscal targets, with the deficit near 5% of GDP and tourism and revenue ahead of target.
Urged cutting electricity import costs by moving to other energy sources and not counting on donor grants.
Said projects in his constituency are slowed by shortages of workers and materials.

speakers.name: Ibrahim Naseem
positions: Noted recurrent spending now roughly matches revenue, which he called reassuring, and urged cutting recurrent costs.
Argued raising tax rates encourages avoidance and that widening the tax base, including untaxed tourism operators, would raise more.
Doubted new revenue sources besides tourism and fishing will arrive quickly.

speakers.name: Hussain Sameer
positions: Said the MVR 64.2 billion budget shows no plan or policy and that a large share goes to debt.
Said PSIP projects in his constituency are progressing slowly, citing the health centre, harbour and roads in Thoddoo.
Raised erosion and harbour delays on nearby islands such as Rasdhoo and Ukulhas.

speakers.name: Mohamed Ismail
positions: Thanked the Finance Minister and said the budget sets out debt, revenue and recurrent costs clearly.
Rejected claims that PSIP projects are not proceeding, citing works under way on islands across the country.
Welcomed funds in the budget for Vilimale' development, housing, health and education.

speakers.name: Mohamed Niushad
positions: Called the MVR 64.2 billion budget imaginary and said state debt will reach about MVR 158 billion by end of 2025 and 175 billion after 2026.
Said presidential pledges for Keyodhoo and Rakeedhoo, such as a health centre, school building and harbour reclamation, have not started.

speakers.name: Ibrahim Hussain
positions: Said much of the budget goes to repay loans taken by the previous government and listed 2025 achievements such as the airport and bridge.
Welcomed increased allowances for single parents and people with disabilities and planned housing and plots.
Said opposition criticism is not based on evidence and projects are under way across islands.

speakers.name: Mauroof Zakir
positions: Said the constitutional amendment should have been split by article and that atoll councils should not be abolished.
Argued abolishing atoll councils weakens decentralisation and shifts power toward the President.
Said PNC members follow the President and group leader rather than their constituents.

speakers.name: Hussain Ziyad
positions: Said atoll councils came from citizens' own efforts and that five years is not long enough to judge them.
Argued atoll members should speak for atolls, citing the dollar, cigarette duty and pay changes as policy shocks.
Warned the Constitution should not be changed whenever convenient.

speakers.name: Hassan Zareer
positions: Said democracy means following the majority and that voters chose this direction.
Argued councils would work directly with ministries once the atoll tier is removed, and that past arrangements left some atolls behind.

speakers.name: Abdul Gafoor Moosa
positions: Opposed abolishing the atoll councils, calling it an assertion of power over people's rights.
Questioned whether this is the democracy voters asked for and said people will make their voice heard.

speakers.name: Mohamed Dawoodh
positions: Supported abolition, citing unclear roles and paperwork confusion between the atoll council and Kulhudhuffushi city council, and land held under the atoll council.
Raised concern for atoll council staff and asked for a dedicated budget so they can do administrative work for other offices.

speakers.name: Saudulla Hilmy
positions: Supported abolition, saying the atoll council's role is small and overlaps with island and city councils, as seen in Thinadhoo.
Said staff worries are real but expected the government to place them in jobs on their own islands.

speakers.name: Mohamed Mamdooh
positions: Said the committee report took on concerns raised by all parties, including those of atoll council staff.
Said decentralisation law amendments would keep atoll assets and money within the islands of that atoll.

decisions: The Speaker closed the debate on the Budget Review Committee's report on the 2026 state budget because the remaining members who wished to speak were in committee.

The House moved on to debate the whole-House committee's report on the constitutional amendment bill; the Speaker said no further amendments had been received and set about one hour of total debate time split between parties.
A break was held from 10:28 to 11:02 and the sitting resumed with the Speaker presiding.
Chair closed the debate on the whole-House committee report on the Constitution amendment bill.
2026 state budget (about MVR 64.2 billion) passed by the House.
Constitution amendment bill passed by the House.
Next sitting set for 9:00 on Wednesday 26 November 2025.

votes.what: 2026 state budget (86 voted; 44 needed to pass; 87 present of 93 members)
Constitution amendment bill as decided by the whole-House committee (87 voted; 70 needed to pass; 87 present of 93 members)
